title: Atomic bombing of Hiroshima
summary: On 6 August 1945, the United States dropped the Little Boy atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan, detonating 600 metres above Shima Hospital and killing between 90,000 and 166,000 people by year's end in history's first combat nuclear attack.
card: At 8:15 a.m. local time, the American B-29 Superfortress Enola Gay released a gun-type uranium fission bomb that exploded over central Hiroshima with the explosive energy of roughly twenty thousand tons of TNT. The resulting shockwave, several-thousand-degree thermal radiation, and violent firestorm obliterated eleven square kilometres of the delta city, inflicting catastrophic acute trauma, severe burns, and fatal radiation sickness. Together with the atomic bombing of Nagasaki three days later and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, the strike compelled Japan's unconditional surrender and inaugurated the nuclear weapons era.
what:
On the morning of 6 August 1945, the United States Army Air Forces carried out the first offensive nuclear strike in history against the Japanese city of Hiroshima. The B-29 Superfortress Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul W. Tibbets Jr. of the 509th Composite Group, took off from Tinian in the Mariana Islands carrying Little Boy, an enriched uranium gun-type atomic weapon. Visual bombing was aimed at the distinctive T-shaped Aioi Bridge. At 8:15 a.m. Japan Standard Time, the weapon detonated approximately 600 metres (c. 1,970 feet) in the air directly above Shima Hospital, roughly 150 metres southeast of the intended bridge target.

The detonation generated a blazing fireball that expanded to hundreds of metres in radius, driving surface temperatures at the hypocenter to between 3,000°C and 4,000°C. An extreme supersonic pressure wave leveled almost all wooden and brick structures within two kilometres, followed by an immense firestorm covering 4.4 square miles (roughly 11 square kilometres) that raged for hours and consumed thousands trapped beneath collapsed buildings. Soon after, toxic soot and radioactive fallout condensed into black rain that showered survivors and relief workers fleeing toward surrounding hills and rivers.

Demographic figures vary considerably across official and scholarly assessments: the Manhattan Engineer District reported an initial tally of 66,000 dead, whereas the City of Hiroshima estimates that 140,000 (plus or minus 10,000) citizens had died by late December 1945, and the Radiation Effects Research Foundation (RERF) calculates 90,000 to 166,000 acute deaths occurring within two to four months. The victims included tens of thousands of school children mobilized for building demolition, Japanese military personnel garrisoned at Second General Army headquarters, Allied prisoners of war, and an estimated tens of thousands of colonized Korean residents and forced laborers. Surviving victims (hibakusha) suffered chronic keloid scarring, cataracts, hematological disorders, and elevated lifetime risks of leukemia and solid cancers, giving rise to a global movement for nuclear disarmament.
how:
The bombing resulted from strategic decisions finalized at the Potsdam Conference and years of nuclear physics development under the Manhattan Project. Little Boy was a gun-type fission weapon containing approximately 64 kilograms of uranium enriched to weapons grade; inside the casing, a conventional explosive propellant fired an enriched uranium projectile down a smoothbore gun barrel into an enriched uranium target insert, initiating an explosive nuclear chain reaction in which approximately one kilogram underwent fission.

On 6 August 1945, the 509th Composite Group dispatched weather planes ahead of the strike aircraft. The primary target, Hiroshima, presented clear visibility. Japanese radar detected incoming aircraft around 7:00 a.m., but because only three B-29 aircraft approached, operators assumed a routine reconnaissance flight and lifted the public air raid warning near 8:00 a.m. Released at 31,600 feet (9,630 metres) at 8:15 a.m. local time, Little Boy fell for 43 seconds before internal radar altimeters and barometric switches triggered the detonator at 600 metres altitude.

The resulting burst released immense energy: 50% in blast pressure, 35% in thermal radiation, and 15% in nuclear radiation. Within one second, the fireball expanded to over 200 metres in radius, radiating intense thermal energy that ignited spontaneous fires across thousands of residential dwellings. The overpressure wave blew outward at hundreds of metres per second, shattering windows up to 12 miles away and collapsing nearly all buildings within a one-mile radius except heavily reinforced concrete structures like the Industrial Promotion Hall (now the Genbaku Dome). Within twenty minutes, rising heat generated strong inward gale-force winds, creating a devastating firestorm that peaked into the afternoon.
why_it_matters:
The bombing of Hiroshima fundamentally restructured global geopolitics, military strategy, and human perceptions of technological vulnerability. Together with the atomic bombing of Nagasaki on 9 August and the simultaneous Soviet offensive across Manchuria, the destruction broke the imperial cabinet's political deadlock, prompting Emperor Hirohito to broadcast Japan's surrender on 15 August and officially conclude World War II. The strike demonstrated that a single aircraft could obliterate an entire urban metropolis in seconds, shifting sovereign power toward states possessing atomic arsenals and sparking the bilateral nuclear arms race that defined the four-decade Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union.

The unprecedented civilian suffering spurred revolutionary changes in international humanitarian law. Witnessing the utter annihilation of non-combatants and medical facilities in Hiroshima encouraged the codification of the 1949 Fourth Geneva Convention, which established comprehensive protections for civilian populations during wartime. Epidemiological investigations into surviving hibakusha conducted by the Atomic Bomb Casualty Commission and the Radiation Effects Research Foundation established foundational global standards for radiation protection, occupational dosimetry, and oncological risk assessment.

Without the atomic bombings, the United States planned to launch Operation Downfall, beginning with amphibious landings on Kyushu in November 1945; Allied military planners anticipated hundreds of thousands of combat casualties, while continuing conventional naval blockade and incendiary bombing would have killed hundreds of thousands more Japanese civilians. Conversely, had the United States opted for a non-combat demonstration or modified its unconditional surrender terms earlier to guarantee the imperial institution, Japan might have capitulated without introducing nuclear weapons into combat history, potentially altering the pace and terrifying brinkmanship of early Cold War nuclear proliferation.

uncertainty.note: Detonation time is established to the minute (8:15 a.m. JST / 23:15 UTC on 5 August); year-end casualty estimates span through 31 December 1945.

related.because: The Manhattan Project researched, designed, and manufactured the Little Boy uranium fission weapon dropped on Hiroshima.
The catastrophic civilian destruction produced by urban atomic bombing motivated post-war expansion of civilian protections in the Fourth Geneva Convention.

beats.caption: At 8:15 a.m. local time, Little Boy detonates approximately 600 meters above Shima Hospital.
Within twenty minutes, spontaneous fires coalesce into a violent firestorm covering 4.4 square miles.
By the end of 1945, an estimated 90,000 to 166,000 people perish from blast, burns, and radiation; nine days later Japan surrenders.

perspectives.holder: United States leadership (President Harry S. Truman, Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson)
perspectives.account: The operational use of the atomic bomb against Hiroshima was a necessary military measure to compel immediate Japanese surrender without an amphibious invasion of the home islands, thereby saving hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers and Japanese casualties.

perspectives.holder: Critical and revisionist historians; nuclear abolitionist hibakusha
perspectives.account: Japan was already militarily exhausted and facing imminent collapse from naval blockade and conventional bombing; the Soviet entry into the war was the primary decisive factor in surrender, rendering the atomic obliteration of an inhabited city unnecessary, disproportionate, and primarily aimed at intimidating the Soviet Union in the emerging Cold War.

audience_note: Contains historical documentation of nuclear weapon detonation, severe burn and radiation injuries, mass civilian casualties, and extensive urban destruction.

importance.justification: The first operational detonation of a nuclear weapon in human history, precipitating the atomic age, ending World War II, and transforming modern warfare, international diplomacy, and civilian vulnerability.
